newsitem.title: USA: Odds-on favorite is Clinton, but some like Socks.
newsitem.headline: Odds-on favorite is Clinton, but some like Socks.

text.p: The prevailing political winds favouring Bill Clinton over Bob Dole have extended across the Atlantic, with a British oddsmaker putting Dole's chances at six to one. Still, some children prefer Socks the Cat.

"It's still almost a certainty that Clinton is going to win according to our betting," said Ian Wassell, the chief spokesman for Ladbroke's of London, which had declined to take bets that Clinton would win for the last 10 days or so.
But due to a surge in bets favouring Republican candidate Dole, Ladbroke's put Clinton back on the boards on Thursday -- but at one-to-10 odds.
"We've taken bets up to ($3,200) (for Dole) which means there is still life in the betting," Wassell said by telephone from London. "A week is a long time in politics."
Reform Party candidate Ross Perot, who had been pressed by the Dole campaign to quit the race, was stable at 50 to one odds.
There are no official U.S. odds for betting on the presidential race, according to Caesar's Palace in Las Vegas.

If the betting were among children, the outcome in the presidential contest might be the same as the one among adults: a light-hearted poll of 443 youngsters aged 8 to 12 showed 56 percent would vote for Clinton over Dole, who pulled 38 percent.

But for real landslide numbers, children gave their votes in fantasy match-ups, showing that basketball star Michael Jordan would trounce pop star Michael Jackson, 80 percent to 19 percent. Actress Whoopi Goldberg would beat "Clueless" actress Alicia Silverstone, 73 percent to 24 percent.
Socks the Cat took 51 percent of the vote in a make-believe contest with television actor Andrew Shue, who got 41 percent. Princess Diana of Britain beat new mother Madonna, 55 percent to 41 percent.

The poll, taken for the Sea World/Busch Gardens theme parks, also found that the two most important issues for the president to address were the environment and world peace. Other important issues were providing better health care, improving schools and helping people get jobs.
On the campaign trail, even eating is political.

President Clinton curried favour with two ethnic groups within 12 hours this week, lunching at the Polish Village Cafe in Detroit's Hamtramck district and eating a midnight dessert at the Versailles Cuban Restaurant in Miami's Little Havana.

Clinton was greeted by enthusiastic crowds in Hamtramck, a once solidly Polish neighbourhood that is now ethnically diverse, but got a mixed welcome in Little Havana, where dozens of Dole and Clinton supporters staged a shouting match.
Chants of "Viva Dole" and "No more lies" were countered by shouts of "Dole no, Clinton si" and "Four more years."

Clinton's appearance in Little Havana cut no ice with Frank Rodriguez, a Yankees baseball fan from Union City, New Jersey, who skipped the third game of the World Series to berate Clinton outside the restaurant for his Cuban policy.
Asked his view of the president's visiting Little Havana, Rodriguez replied with a single word: "Pandering."
